Tab 1 • Orientation only

How to think through aerobic cocci

The lecture is organized as a sequence of identification decisions: first separate Gram-positive from Gram-negative cocci, then use a small set of laboratory tests and clinical patterns to reach the organism.

pp. 1–11

Central question

Core ideaGiven a coccus, which combination of Gram reaction, arrangement, enzyme test, hemolysis, selective sensitivity, sugar fermentation, and clinical setting identifies it?
BRANCH 1Gram-positive cocci
BRANCH 2Staphylococcus
BRANCH 3Streptococcus
BRANCH 4Gram-negative Neisseria

The lecture repeatedly returns to one practical rule: identify the organism by combining the test result with the clinical picture—not by using one finding in isolation.

High-yield anchors

  • Catalase: Staphylococcus (+) vs Streptococcus (−).
  • Coagulase: S. aureus (+).
  • Novobiocin: S. saprophyticus resistant; S. epidermidis sensitive.
  • Optochin: S. pneumoniae sensitive; viridans resistant.
  • Bacitracin: S. pyogenes sensitive; S. agalactiae resistant.
  • Maltose: N. meningitidis ferments it; N. gonorrhoeae does not.

What this flow means: the lecture uses a branching diagnostic framework. Each test narrows the possibilities until the organism’s virulence factors and disease pattern make sense.

How the topics connect

Identification tells you which organism is present. Its virulence factors then explain how it survives or spreads. Those mechanisms produce the characteristic clinical syndromes. Finally, the lecture links the organism to its diagnostic specimen, treatment, prophylaxis, or prevention.

The identification logic

Start broad, then narrow. The tests are not random facts; each one answers a specific branching question.

pp. 1, 2, 5, 8–10

Gram-positive cocci: the first fork

Simple ideaCatalase separates the two major Gram-positive coccal genera in this lecture.
Complete explanationStaphylococci produce catalase, which breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. A positive test foams. Streptococcus and Enterococcus lack this ability, so the test shows no reaction.
High-yield takeawayClusters + catalase positive → Staphylococcus. Pairs/chains + catalase negative → Streptococcus.
CATALASE +Staphylococcus
→
COAGULASE +S. aureus
/
COAGULASE −Novobiocin
Resistant = saprophyticus
Sensitive = epidermidis

Streptococci: use hemolysis as the second fork

PatternWhat happens to RBCsPlate appearanceLecture organismsNext discriminator
AlphaPartial breakdownGreenish clearingS. pneumoniae, viridansOptochin: sensitive vs resistant
BetaComplete breakdownClear zoneS. pyogenes, S. agalactiaeBacitracin: sensitive vs resistant
GammaNo breakdownPlate stays redEnterococcus, S. bovisGrowth in 6.5% NaCl: growth vs no growth
Do not confuseAlpha does not mean “strongest.” It means partial hemolysis. Beta is complete. Gamma is none.

Alpha-hemolytic branch

  • S. pneumoniae: encapsulated, optochin sensitive, bile soluble.
  • Viridans: no capsule in the lecture’s comparison, optochin resistant, bile insoluble.
Recall cuepneumOniae → Optochin sensitive. viRidians → Resistant.

Beta-hemolytic branch

  • S. pyogenes: Group A, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive.
  • S. agalactiae: Group B, bacitracin resistant, PYR negative, hippurate positive.
Recall cue“Trace the genes of pyogenes” for bacitracin sensitivity; Group B strep has Bacitracin Bad.

Gram-negative cocci: Neisseria

Both organisms are Gram-negative diplococci and oxidase positive. The lecture’s key differentiators are the polysaccharide capsule and the maltose fermentation test.

FeatureN. gonorrhoeaeN. meningitidis
FermentationGlucose onlyGlucose + maltose
CapsuleAbsentPresent
Typical lecture location/diseaseGenital infectionURTI → meningitis
Maltose brothStays redTurns yellow

Lock It In

Core concept: every test is a branch point. Main differentiator: catalase starts Gram-positive coccal identification. Key sequence: catalase → coagulase/hemolysis → disc or sugar test. Exam cue: do not stop at “alpha hemolytic”—use optochin to finish the identification.
Staphylococcus aureus

From colonizer to invasive pathogen

S. aureus is part of normal skin and nasal flora in about one quarter of the population, yet can cause disease when bacterial load rises or barriers are disrupted.

pp. 1–3

What it is

  • Gram-positive coccus, usually in clusters (“golden cluster of grapes”), but may appear singly, in pairs, tetrads, or chains.
  • About 1 μm; golden-yellow colonies on blood agar.
  • Facultative anaerobe, non-motile, non-spore-forming.
  • Young cocci stain strongly Gram-positive; aging cultures may become Gram-negative.
  • Catalase positive and coagulase positive.
Why it mattersThe organism may remain a harmless colonizer, cause disease by direct invasion, produce disease by toxins, or combine both mechanisms.

Colonization → infection

LOW LOADIntact skin
Colonization
→
HIGH LOAD + BREAKEczema, shaving, cuts, surgery
Active infection

The key idea: progression depends on skin integrity + bacterial load.

Catalase and coagulase: what the tests are showing

Catalase

Hydrogen peroxide is broken into water + oxygen. Visible foam means the organism is catalase positive.

Coagulase

Extracellular coagulase converts soluble fibrinogen → fibrin. Sticky fibrin creates visible clumps and helps distinguish S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.

Virulence factors as a coordinated strategy

FactorFunction
Protein ABinds the Fc portion of IgG, interfering with opsonization; also described as an adhesin promoting attachment and invasion.
Polysaccharide capsuleAnti-phagocytic; resists PMNs.
CoagulaseConverts fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a coat.
HyaluronidaseDigests hyaluronic acid and promotes spread.
StaphylokinaseDissolves fibrin clots, freeing bacteria.
Teichoic acidsImportant in cell-wall metabolism.

How localized infection progresses

  • Localized: pimple / follicular infection / abscess after contamination of a wound.
  • Progression: pimple → furuncle (boil) → carbuncle (cluster of furuncles).
  • Impetigo: epidermis.
  • Cellulitis: reaches dermis and spreads rapidly.
  • Subcutaneous abscess: walled-off pus; may develop septations.
  • Non-skin abscesses may occur in the mouth, liver, kidney, spleen, or brain.

Dissemination: what happens after bloodstream entry

1Bacteremia
Bacteria enter blood.
→
2Widespread immune reaction
Vasodilation and pressure drop.
→
3Hypotension + poor perfusion
Sepsis.
→
4Seeding of organs
CNS, lungs, heart valves, bone, joints, muscle.
SiteCondition
MusclePyomyositis
BoneOsteomyelitis
Joint spaceSeptic arthritis
Bloodstream with infected clotSeptic thrombophlebitis
CNSMeningitis or epidural abscess
LungSevere pneumonia
Heart valvesInfective endocarditis with vegetations and embolization

Biofilm: why device infections persist

Simple ideaA biofilm is a protected bacterial community on an implanted surface.
Complete explanationS. aureus produces an extracellular matrix of exopolysaccharides (EPS). Within it, cells communicate through biochemical signals and exchange genetic material, including antibiotic-resistance genes. The lecture notes that S. aureus thrives but does not divide rapidly inside the biofilm.
Clinical meaningSlow growth and matrix barriers reduce antibiotic effectiveness. Device-associated infection may persist and often requires attention to the colonized surface.

Diagnostic approach

  • Culture specimens: surface swab, pus/abscess aspirate, blood, endotracheal aspirate, sputum, spinal fluid.
  • Colonization specimen: nasal swab.
  • Gram stain: gram-positive cocci in clusters may be seen in pus or sputum, but Gram stain alone cannot distinguish pathogenic S. aureus from nonaureus species such as S. epidermidis.

Lock It In

Core concept: S. aureus is both a colonizer and an invasive/toxin-producing pathogen. Differentiator: coagulase positive. Sequence: skin break or high load → local infection → bloodstream → sepsis/organ seeding. Exam cue: catheter + thick extracellular matrix + persistent infection = biofilm.
S. aureus extensions

Toxins, resistance, treatment, and other staphylococci

This section separates toxin-mediated disease from invasive disease, then explains why beta-lactam and vancomycin resistance matter.

pp. 3–4

Toxins: connect mechanism to syndrome

ToxinMechanism in lectureResult / recognition pattern
TSST-1Produced at infection site, enters bloodstream, binds MHC class II → cytokine stormToxic shock syndrome: abrupt high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, scarlatiniform/sunburn-like rash, hypotension; severe cardiac/renal failure. Linked to high-absorbency tampons and staph wound infection.
Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL)Phage-encoded; pore formation lyses WBCs → increased cation permeability → release of IL-8, leukotriene, histamineNecrosis and severe inflammation
Alpha hemolysinTargets eukaryotic membranesMembrane injury
Beta hemolysinDegrades sphingomyelinRBC-toxic
Delta hemolysinDisrupts membranesDiarrheal disease
Gamma hemolysin / leukocidinLyses WBCsLeukocyte destruction
Exfoliative toxins A & BDissolve mucopolysaccharide matrix of epidermisRitter’s disease / staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: generalized desquamation
Enterotoxins15 types; heat-stable, resistant to gut enzymes, withstand 100°CFood poisoning: 1–8 h incubation, violent nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, rapid recovery, no fever

Beta-lactam resistance: follow the target

NORMAL TARGETPBP / DD-transpeptidase
Cross-links NAG-NAM peptidoglycan strands.
→
BETA-LACTAMPBP disrupted
No cross-linking → leaky wall → death.
→
COUNTER 1Beta-lactamase
Breaks beta-lactam ring.
→
COUNTER 2mecA / SCCmec
Special PBP that beta-lactams cannot bind.

This explains why: beta-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanic acid block beta-lactamase, but methicillin resistance is independent of beta-lactamase and instead involves the SCCmec gene cassette.

SCCmec patternTypes I, II, III, VI, VIII are linked to HA-MRSA; type IV is linked to CA-MRSA in the lecture.

Resistance vocabulary

  • Tolerance: drug inhibits but does not kill; large gap between minimal inhibitory and minimal lethal concentration.
  • Plasmid-mediated resistance to tetracyclines, erythromycins, and aminoglycosides is common.
  • Nearly all S. aureus strains now produce beta-lactamase.
  • VISA: intermediate vancomycin resistance.
  • VRSA: complete vancomycin resistance.

Treatment and control as stated in the lecture

  • Clinically significant isolates should undergo antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
  • Abscesses and closed suppurating lesions require drainage.
  • Careful local antiseptic care helps prevent recurrent skin abscesses.
  • Long-term corticosteroid use should be avoided whenever possible.
  • The lecture lists clindamycin and vancomycin as common MRSA treatments, with alternatives including tetracycline, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, linezolid, tigecycline, daptomycin, and quinupristin-dalfopristin.
  • Control relies on surveillance and strict contact precautions, especially in newborn nurseries, ICUs, ORs, and cancer chemotherapy wards.
Lecture-specific noteThe reviewer preserves the lecture’s treatment statements. The lecture emphasizes testing the isolate and choosing the antibiotic according to susceptibility.

S. epidermidis

  • Coagulase negative
  • Novobiocin sensitive
  • Important virulence factor: biofilm
  • Causes implanted-device infections, especially in very young, old, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Hard to cure because organisms hide within biofilm and are often drug resistant.

S. saprophyticus

  • Coagulase negative
  • Novobiocin resistant
  • Associated with UTIs in young women.
Key differentiatorAmong coagulase-negative staphylococci: saprophyticus = resistant; epidermidis = sensitive.

Lock It In

Core concept: S. aureus disease may be toxin-mediated or invasive. Differentiator: enterotoxin gives rapid afebrile GI illness; TSST-1 gives shock and rash. Mechanism: mecA changes the PBP target. Exam cue: implanted device + CoNS = S. epidermidis biofilm.
Streptococcus framework

Classify first, then identify

Streptococci are Gram-positive, catalase-negative cocci in pairs or chains. The lecture classifies them by hemolysis, Lancefield antigen, laboratory reactions, ecology, and clinical pattern.

pp. 4–5

What the blood agar pattern means

Simple ideaBlood agar shows how much the organism breaks down hemoglobin around the colony.
Complete explanationAlpha hemolysis leaves a greenish zone because breakdown is partial. Beta hemolysis clears RBCs completely. Gamma hemolysis produces no visible change.
High-yield takeawayHemolysis narrows the group, but a second test completes identification.

Lancefield classification

The lecture describes a serologic system based on detecting the group-specific carbohydrate antigen in the streptococcal cell wall. The specificity is determined by an amino sugar and groups run from A to W, excluding I and J.

GroupAmino sugar / substance stated in lectureKey organism
ARhamnose–N-acetylglucosamineS. pyogenes
BRhamnose–glucosamineS. agalactiae
CRhamnose–N-acetylgalactosamineOther streptococci
DGlycerol teichoic acid containing D-alanine and glucoseEnterococcus / S. bovis grouping
EGlucopyranosyl–N-acetylgalactosamineLecture table category

Complete identification pathway

CATALASE −Streptococcus
→
ALPHAOptochin
Sensitive: pneumoniae
Resistant: viridans
/
BETABacitracin
Sensitive: pyogenes
Resistant: agalactiae
/
GAMMA6.5% NaCl
Growth: Enterococcus
No growth: S. bovis

What this flow means: one visual property—hemolysis—creates three branches. A targeted confirmatory test then separates the organisms within that branch.

Lock It In

Core concept: hemolysis is a classification step, not the final diagnosis. Differentiator: optochin for alpha; bacitracin for beta. Sequence: catalase negative → hemolysis → confirmatory test. Exam cue: group A = pyogenes; group B = agalactiae.
Streptococcus pneumoniae

The encapsulated alpha-hemolytic pneumococcus

The capsule links the organism’s laboratory identity to its major clinical risk: susceptibility in patients who cannot effectively clear encapsulated organisms.

pp. 5–6

Defining characteristics

  • Gram positive, catalase negative
  • Alpha hemolytic
  • Optochin sensitive
  • Encapsulated with polysaccharide capsule
  • Lance-shaped diplococci in chains
  • Bile soluble, facultative anaerobe, glucose fermenter
  • Found in the nasopharynx; normal inhabitant of the upper respiratory tract
Key differentiatorBoth S. pneumoniae and viridans are alpha hemolytic. The lecture’s definitive discriminator is optochin sensitivity.

Virulence factor 1: polysaccharide capsule

CAPSULEResists phagocytosis
→
NORMAL SPLEENC3b opsonization
Pathogen is tagged.
→
SPLENIC MACROPHAGESRecognize the tag
Engulf and destroy.

In anatomic or functional asplenia, the lecture states that this protective process fails. Anatomic asplenia follows removal or physical loss of the spleen; functional asplenia occurs when the spleen remains but does not work, as described with sickle-cell occlusive injury.

Clinical meaningSudden fever, fatigue, malaise, sepsis, or death in a patient with anatomic or functional asplenia should prompt consideration of encapsulated organisms. S. pneumoniae is linked to OPSI—overwhelming postsplenectomy infection.

Virulence factor 2: IgA protease

IgA is the lecture’s first-line antibody on mucosal surfaces such as the nose, throat, lungs, and ears. S. pneumoniae produces IgA protease, which cleaves IgA and makes mucosal invasion easier.

  • Meningitis
  • Otitis media
  • Pneumonia
  • Sinusitis
Lecture recall cues.pneuMOPSIae links MOPS with OPSI.

Clinical pattern

  • Pneumococcal pneumonia begins suddenly with fever, chills, and sharp pleural pain.
  • Sputum is characteristically bloody or rust-colored.
  • Lowered host resistance predisposes to pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis, bronchitis, bacteremia, meningitis, peritonitis, and other infections listed in the lecture.
If you see X, think YRust-colored sputum → S. pneumoniae.

Antigenic structure and loss of resistance

  • Capsular polysaccharide prevents or delays ingestion by phagocytes.
  • Quellung reaction: capsule swells when mixed with specific anti-polysaccharide serum; organisms agglutinate through antibody cross-linking.
  • An URTI may damage surface cells and cause abnormal mucus accumulation that protects pneumococci from phagocytosis.
  • Other lecture-listed predisposing conditions include malnutrition, general debility, sickle cell anemia, hyposplenism, nephrosis, and complement deficiency.

Diagnosis

  • Blood: culture
  • CSF and sputum: smear and culture

Treatment and prevention

  • Routine susceptibility testing to select penicillin, macrolide, or third-generation cephalosporin.
  • The lecture states vaccines induce antibodies to capsular polysaccharides.
  • It also states predisposing factors are more important than exposure, and a healthy carrier may disseminate pneumococci more than a sick patient.

Lock It In

Core concept: the capsule explains virulence and asplenia risk. Differentiator: alpha hemolytic + optochin sensitive + bile soluble. Sequence: capsule evades phagocytosis; C3b/splenic clearance normally counters it. Exam cue: rust sputum or postsplenectomy sepsis = pneumococcus.
Viridans streptococci

Oral adhesion and damaged-valve colonization

Viridans is an umbrella group in the lecture, including S. mutans, S. mitis, and S. sanguinis. Its disease pattern follows from where it normally lives: the oropharynx.

pp. 6–7

Defining characteristics

  • Gram positive, catalase negative
  • Alpha hemolytic
  • Optochin resistant
  • Chain-like growth
  • Bile insoluble
  • Facultative anaerobe
  • Found in the oropharynx
Do not confuseS. pneumoniae is associated with the nasopharynx; viridans with the oropharynx in the lecture.

Two virulence patterns

Biofilms

Promote adhesion in the oral cavity and cause gingivitis. Examples: S. mutans and S. mitis.

Lecture cue: “Mute (mutans) = mouth = gingivitis.”

Dextrans

Bind to fibrin-platelet aggregates on damaged heart valves. Example: S. sanguinis.

Lecture cue: “sanguine = blood = endocarditis.”

How subacute bacterial endocarditis develops

1Oral manipulation
Normal oral flora enter blood.
→
2Bacteremia
Organisms travel hematogenously.
→
3Damaged valve
Fibrin-platelet aggregates provide a surface.
→
4Dextran-mediated adhesion
Vegetation develops.

Clinical meaning: the organism is not primarily identified by a destructive exotoxin. Its key advantage is adhesion to abnormal endocardium and biofilm-like persistence.

Treatment statement in the lecture

The lecture lists amoxicillin prophylaxis for patients at high risk of developing subacute endocarditis.

Lock It In

Core concept: oral flora cause disease by adhesion. Differentiator: alpha hemolytic but optochin resistant. Sequence: oral entry → bacteremia → damaged valve → dextran-mediated vegetation. Exam cue: dental/oral source + abnormal valve = viridans.
Streptococcus pyogenes • Group A

A beta-hemolytic organism with direct and immune-mediated disease

The lecture emphasizes that S. pyogenes has many virulence factors and produces both acute infections and delayed immune complications.

p. 7

Defining characteristics

  • Gram positive, catalase negative
  • Beta hemolytic
  • Bacitracin sensitive
  • Lancefield Group A
  • PYR positive
  • Chains; found in the nasopharynx and associated with pharyngitis
Recall cue“Trace the genes of pyogenes” → bacitracin sensitive.

Virulence factors

  • M protein: inhibits and degrades C3b; involved in molecular mimicry.
  • Hyaluronic acid capsule: inhibits phagocytosis; camouflage for immune evasion.
  • Lipoteichoic acid: adhesion to host cells.
  • Protein F: fibronectin-binding protein that promotes epithelial attachment.
  • Streptokinase: dissolves fibrin clots.

Clinical syndromes: organize them by mechanism

PatternSyndromeLecture clues
Upper respiratoryPharyngitisTonsillar inflammation ± exudate, fever, lymphadenopathy; common in toddlers and young children. Penicillin is given to prevent rheumatic fever.
Delayed immuneAcute rheumatic fever2–4 weeks after infection; migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum.
Delayed immunePoststreptococcal glomerulonephritisAfter pharyngitis or impetigo; high ASO, low C3; immune-complex deposition; hematuria, HTN, edema, oliguria; “lumpy-bumpy” IF.
SkinImpetigoHoney-crusted lesions on erythematous base; typically non-bullous.
Deep soft tissueNecrotizing fasciitisListed severe invasive syndrome.
SkinErysipelasWell-demarcated, inflamed, usually raised patches/plaques ± lymphangitis.
Toxin / hypersensitivityScarlet feverPharyngitis, fever, flushing, strawberry tongue, sandpaper rash sparing palms/soles, circumoral pallor; linked to delayed hypersensitivity to erythrogenic toxin A.

Acute rheumatic fever: molecular mimicry

1Immune response to M protein
Antibodies and T cells form.
→
2Structural similarity
M protein resembles cardiac myosin.
→
3Cross-reaction
Immune cells attack cardiac and other tissues.
→
4Inflammation
Heart, joints, skin, CNS.
Exam trap from the lectureARF follows respiratory/throat infection only, whereas PSGN may follow either respiratory or skin infection.

Lecture mnemonic: PyAGINES

Pharyngitis • Acute rheumatic fever • Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis • Impetigo • Necrotizing fasciitis • Erysipelas • Scarlet fever

Treatment statements

The lecture lists penicillin, first- or second-generation cephalosporins, and a macrolide when allergic to penicillin.

Lock It In

Core concept: S. pyogenes causes direct infections and post-infectious immune disease. Differentiator: Group A, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive. Mechanism: M-protein molecular mimicry explains ARF. Exam cue: honey crust, sandpaper rash, or migratory polyarthritis after throat infection.
Streptococcus agalactiae • Group B

Maternal colonization and neonatal invasive disease

The lecture connects the organism’s normal location in the female genital tract to transmission during vaginal delivery.

p. 8

Defining characteristics

  • Gram positive, catalase negative
  • Beta hemolytic
  • Bacitracin resistant
  • Lancefield Group B
  • PYR negative
  • Hippurate positive
  • Chains; facultative anaerobe
  • Found in the female genital tract; normal vaginal and lower GI flora

Lecture recall pattern

Group B StrepBacitracin Bad (negative/resistant) • Byrrolidonyl Bad (PYR negative) • hiBurate (hippurate positive) • Babies
  • CAMP factor: used as an identification test; enlarges the hemolysis area with S. aureus. The lecture notes it is not really considered a virulence factor.
  • Capsule: listed virulence factor.

Why neonates are the focus

1Maternal vaginal colonization
→
2Baby passes through birth canal
→
3Exposure to S. agalactiae
→
4Sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis

Lecture mnemonic: SPM = Swab Pregnant Mothers; also Sepsis, Pneumonia, Meningitis.

Screening and treatment

  • Screen pregnant mothers at 35–37 weeks.
  • Use vaginal and rectal swabs.
  • If positive: intrapartum penicillin.
  • Drug of choice: Penicillin G.

Adults at risk

Elderly and immunocompromised adults are at greatest risk for invasive disease. Predisposing factors listed in the lecture include diabetes, cancer, advanced age, liver cirrhosis, corticosteroid therapy, HIV, and other immunocompromised states.

Major manifestations in descending frequency: bacteremia, skin/soft-tissue infection, respiratory infection, and genitourinary infection.

Lock It In

Core concept: maternal colonization creates neonatal exposure. Differentiator: Group B, bacitracin resistant, PYR negative, hippurate positive. Sequence: colonized mother → birth canal exposure → neonatal SPM. Exam cue: 35–37-week vaginal/rectal swab.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

A nonencapsulated diplococcus that survives at mucosal surfaces

The organism uses pili, antigenic variation, IgA protease, catalase, LOS, and membrane proteins to attach, evade, injure, and disseminate.

pp. 8–10

Microbe anatomy and physiology

  • Gram-negative oval diplococci, about 0.8 μm, side-by-side like coffee beans.
  • Thin peptidoglycan does not retain crystal violet; stains pink with safranin.
  • Rapidly killed by drying, sunlight, moist heat, and many disinfectants.
  • Non-motile, non-spore-forming, obligate aerobe.
  • Catalase positive, oxidase positive.
  • No polysaccharide capsule.
  • Ferments glucose only, not maltose.
Key differentiatorN. gonorrhoeae cannot ferment maltose, so phenol-red maltose broth stays red. N. meningitidis ferments maltose and turns the broth yellow.

Laboratory diagnosis

  • Culture is mainly indicated for drug-resistance monitoring and medico-legal cases.
  • Specimens may come from urethra, cervix, rectum, conjunctiva, throat, or synovial fluid, depending on site.
  • Grows on Thayer–Martin agar, a selective chocolate medium with antimicrobials such as vancomycin, nystatin, colistin, and trimethoprim.
  • Repeat Gram stain confirms Gram-negative diplococci; biochemical pattern is oxidase +, catalase +, glucose fermentation +.
  • NAAT provides highly sensitive and specific detection of bacterial genetic material; the lecture also lists co-agglutination and immunofluorescence staining.

Virulence factors as a step-by-step survival plan

FactorWhat it doesWhy it matters
PiliAttach to host mucosa, resist phagocytosis, connect bacteria, enable conjugation/genetic transfer.Major virulence factor; piliated strains are virulent. Antigenic/phase variation prevents a rapid specific immune response and contributes to the lack of an effective vaccine in the lecture.
IgA proteaseDestroys mucosal IgA.Weakens first-line mucosal defense.
CatalaseBreaks down hydrogen peroxide inside the phagosome.Allows survival within neutrophils, replication, rupture, and possible gonococcemia.
LOSTriggers widespread inflammation; causes ciliary loss and mucosal cell death.May produce sepsis. Sialylation creates molecular mimicry by making LOS resemble host glycosphingolipids.
Por proteinPrevents phagosome–lysosome fusion; binds C3b and C4b.Immune evasion.
Opa proteinsAdhesion within colonies and to host receptors.Supports colonization.
Rmp / Protein IIIForms pores; resists antibody–complement activity; interferes with receptor binding on phagocytes.Further immune evasion.

Clinical syndromes

Population/siteLecture manifestations
Male genital infectionUrethritis, prostatitis, epididymitis; burning urination; purulent or bloody urethral discharge.
Female genital infectionUrethritis, vaginitis, cervicitis; thick purulent discharge. Spread to uterus/tubes/ovaries may produce PID.
PID complicationFitz–Hugh–Curtis syndrome: inflammation involving Glisson’s capsule, with “violin-string” adhesions.
NeonateTransmission during vaginal delivery → early neonatal conjunctivitis at 2–5 days, with swollen eyelids and mucopurulent discharge.
Disseminated infectionGonococcemia may cause gonococcal arthritis or endocarditis.

Diagnostic recognition

Vaginal or urethral material on Gram stain may reveal pink coffee-bean-shaped diplococci within neutrophils. Confirm with Thayer–Martin culture or NAAT.

Epidemiology, treatment, prevention

  • Worldwide distribution; sexually transmitted, often from asymptomatic men and women.
  • Lecture first-line: third-generation cephalosporin, ceftriaxone; it specifies 250 mg IM single dose and addition of azithromycin or doxycycline for common Chlamydia coinfection.
  • Prevention: fewer sexual partners, early diagnosis/treatment, contact finding, education and screening, condoms for partial protection.
  • Neonatal ophthalmia prevention/treatment: lecture lists 0.5% erythromycin or 1% tetracycline ophthalmic ointment.
Lecture-specific noteThese doses and prophylaxis statements are reproduced from the lecture source rather than updated with outside guidelines.

Lock It In

Core concept: no capsule, but many surface and immune-evasion mechanisms. Differentiator: glucose only; maltose negative. Sequence: pili attach → IgA protease weakens mucosa → intracellular survival → local or disseminated disease. Exam cue: intracellular coffee-bean diplococci + purulent genital discharge.
Neisseria meningitidis

Nasopharyngeal colonization, bloodstream spread, and fulminant inflammation

The capsule and endotoxin-like LOS explain why the organism can evade phagocytosis yet trigger meningitis, DIC, shock, and adrenal hemorrhage.

pp. 10–11

Defining and laboratory features

  • Gram-negative diplococci
  • Oxidase positive
  • Ferments glucose and maltose
  • Polysaccharide capsule
  • Specimens: blood; CSF and petechial aspirates; nasopharyngeal swab.
  • Smears may show neisseriae inside PMNs or extracellularly.
  • Culture on chocolate agar or selective Thayer–Martin/VCN agar.
  • Serologic antibodies may be measured by latex agglutination, hemagglutination, or bactericidal activity.

Virulence factors

  • Pili: attach to nasopharyngeal epithelium, endothelium, erythrocytes; antigenic variation.
  • IgA protease: cleaves IgA on mucosal surfaces.
  • LOS / lipid A disaccharide: endotoxin; lecture emphasizes LOS, not LPS.
  • Capsule: inhibits phagocytosis; incorporates human sialic-acid derivatives such as NANA for molecular mimicry.
  • PorA/PorB: nutrient diffusion and host-cell interaction.
  • Opa proteins: attachment.
SusceptibilityThe lecture highlights risk in asplenia/sickle cell disease and C5–C9 terminal complement deficiency.

Entry and spread

  1. Humans are the only natural hosts.
  2. Respiratory droplets deliver the organism to the nasopharynx.
  3. Pili attach to the mucosa.
  4. IgA protease helps evade mucosal antibody.
  5. The organism enters blood and spreads hematogenously.

Meningococcal meningitis

1Travel to brain
→
2Cross blood–CSF barrier
→
3Replicate in CSF
→
4Meningeal inflammation
Headache, vomiting, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, phonophobia; may progress to coma within hours.

Disseminated meningococcemia

LOS RELEASEMassive inflammatory response
→
ENDOTHELIUMCapillary leak
+
COAGULATIONDIC
Thrombocytopenia and bleeding
→
CLINICALPetechiae + hypovolemic shock

Fulminant meningococcemia is described as meningitis with high fever and hemorrhagic rash.

Waterhouse–Frederickson syndrome, step by step

  1. Inflammation damages small adrenal vessels.
  2. Endothelium is injured and vessels rupture.
  3. DIC impairs proper clotting, allowing blood to leak into adrenal tissue.
  4. Generalized hypoperfusion adds ischemia and necrosis.
  5. Adrenal destruction produces acute adrenal insufficiency / Addisonian crisis.

Treatment, prophylaxis, vaccine in the lecture

  • Ceftriaxone: treatment.
  • Rifampin: prophylaxis for close contacts.
  • Vaccine described for groups A and C using purified capsular polysaccharide.
  • The lecture states no type B polysaccharide vaccine in this framework because type B is not immunogenic, and notes many worldwide infections are caused by type B.

Lock It In

Core concept: capsule aids survival; LOS drives fulminant inflammation. Differentiator: maltose fermenter and encapsulated. Sequence: nasopharynx → blood → CSF or systemic LOS release. Exam cue: fever + stiff neck + petechial rash or adrenal collapse; close contacts receive rifampin in the lecture.

ARF vs PSGN

  • ARF: follows throat infection only in the lecture; molecular mimicry; heart/joints/skin/CNS.
  • PSGN: follows throat or skin infection; immune-complex deposition; low C3; nephritic findings.

Food poisoning vs toxic shock

  • Enterotoxin: 1–8 h, violent GI symptoms, rapid recovery, no fever.
  • TSST-1: cytokine storm, high fever, rash, hypotension, poor perfusion, possible organ failure.

S. aureus rapid recall

  • Clusters, golden colonies, catalase +, coagulase +
  • Protein A → Fc binding; capsule → antiphagocytic
  • Coagulase → fibrin coat; hyaluronidase → spread; staphylokinase → fibrinolysis
  • Skin: pimple → furuncle → carbuncle; impetigo, cellulitis, abscess
  • Spread: pyomyositis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, septic thrombophlebitis, sepsis, CNS/lung/endocarditis
  • Biofilm → devices, slow growth, poor antibiotic penetration
  • Enterotoxin: 1–8 h, no fever; TSST-1: fever + rash + shock; Exfoliative: Ritter; PVL: necrosis
  • mecA/SCCmec → altered PBP → MRSA

SpeciesKey
aureusCoagulase +; toxins/invasion
epidermidisNovobiocin sensitive; device biofilm
saprophyticusNovobiocin resistant; young-woman UTI

Strep branch points

HemolysisOrganismsFinish with
Alpha = partial/greenpneumoniae vs viridansOptochin: pneumoniae sensitive, viridans resistant
Beta = complete/clearpyogenes vs agalactiaeBacitracin: pyogenes sensitive, agalactiae resistant
Gamma = none/redEnterococcus vs S. bovis6.5% NaCl: Enterococcus grows, S. bovis does not

S. pneumoniae

  • Alpha, optochin sensitive, bile soluble, encapsulated, lance diplococci
  • Capsule → phagocytosis resistance → OPSI risk in asplenia
  • IgA protease → MOPS: meningitis, otitis, pneumonia, sinusitis
  • Rust-colored sputum
  • Quellung = capsular swelling
  • Specimens: blood, CSF, sputum

Viridans

  • Alpha, optochin resistant, bile insoluble, oropharynx
  • Biofilms → oral adhesion/gingivitis
  • Dextrans → fibrin-platelet binding on damaged valves
  • Oral manipulation → bacteremia → subacute endocarditis

S. pyogenes

  • Group A, beta, bacitracin sensitive, PYR +
  • M protein → C3b inhibition + molecular mimicry
  • PyAGINES: pharyngitis, ARF, PSGN, impetigo, nec fasc, erysipelas, scarlet fever
  • ARF after throat only; PSGN after throat or skin
  • Scarlet: strawberry tongue + sandpaper rash

S. agalactiae

  • Group B, beta, bacitracin resistant, PYR −, hippurate +
  • Female genital tract; maternal colonization
  • SPM: sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis
  • Screen 35–37 weeks with vaginal + rectal swab
  • Positive → intrapartum penicillin

N. gonorrhoeae

  • Gram− coffee-bean diplococci, oxidase +, catalase +, glucose only, no capsule
  • Pili: attachment + phase variation + genetic transfer
  • IgA protease; catalase survival in neutrophil; LOS + sialylation
  • Thayer–Martin / NAAT
  • Urethritis/cervicitis/PID; Fitz–Hugh–Curtis; neonatal conjunctivitis 2–5 d; arthritis/endocarditis

N. meningitidis

  • Gram− diplococci, oxidase +, glucose + maltose, capsule
  • Nasopharynx → blood → meningitis/meningococcemia
  • LOS → capillary leak + DIC → petechiae + shock
  • Waterhouse–Frederickson → adrenal hemorrhage/necrosis → adrenal insufficiency
  • Risk: asplenia/sickle cell and C5–C9 deficiency
  • Ceftriaxone; rifampin close-contact prophylaxis
